title: File handling
sub: Worksheet for the 360° experience: Records office
objectives: know how to open a text file, read what is in it and close it again
understand the difference between write mode and append mode
know how to split one line of a file into its separate fields
starter: A program opens scores.txt in write mode, and the file already holds 40 lines of results. Write down what the file holds the moment that line has run, and which mode should have been used to add to it instead.

stations.name: Reading a whole file
stations.fact: A file left open can keep other programs out, and may lose data that was not written yet.
stations.challenge: Why should a program close a file as soon as it has finished with it?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: A file called notes.txt is already there. Read the whole of it in one go, close it, and display exactly what was in it and nothing of your own.
A file called data.txt is already there and may be empty. Read the whole of it and count every character, newlines included, then display characters [the count] and nothing else.

logic.title: Plan the one you found hardest: inputs, what happens to them, what is printed.

stations.name: Reading line by line
stations.fact: A newline is one single invisible character, which is why a stripped line comes out shorter.
stations.challenge: Why is a stripped line one character shorter than the line that was read?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: A file called words.txt is already there and may be empty. Read its first line only, close the file and strip the newline off, then display first [that line], then length [how many characters are left] on the next line.
A file called words.txt is already there with one word per line, and may be empty. Read it and display lines [how many lines it holds] and nothing else.

A file called words.txt is already there with one word per line, and may be empty. Read it and display one line for each word in the form [position] [word], counting from 1, or none on a line of its own when the file holds no words.

logic.title: Plan the one you found hardest: inputs, what happens to them, what is printed.

stations.name: Writing to a file
stations.fact: Write mode creates the file if it is not there, which is handy and dangerous in equal measure.
stations.challenge: What happens to the contents of a file the moment it is opened in w mode?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: Ask the user for a word. Make a file called out.txt, write that word on one line and ready on the next, and close it. Then read out.txt back in one go and display it.

Ask the user for a word. Open the file data.txt in write mode, which empties whatever it held, write that word on a line of its own and close it. Read it back and display [every line in it], then lines [how many] on the last line.

logic.title: Plan the one you found hardest: inputs, what happens to them, what is printed.

stations.name: Adding to a file
stations.fact: Three modes cover everything you need: r to read, w to write from scratch and a to add on the end.
stations.challenge: Which mode would a visitor log use, and why that one?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: Ask the user for a word and add it to the end of the file log.txt on a line of its own, without losing the lines already there. Then read the whole file back and display [every line in it], one on each line, and nothing else.

Ask the user for a word and append it to the file log.txt on a line of its own, without losing the lines already there. Then read the whole file back and display latest [the last line], then total [how many lines] on the next line.

logic.title: Plan the one you found hardest: inputs, what happens to them, what is printed.

stations.name: Records in a file
stations.fact: A file of comma-separated records is a CSV file, and a spreadsheet will open one straight away.
stations.challenge: How does a program find the record for one particular name?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor
head: Program
Marks
Done
rows: A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line, and may be empty. Read it and display one line for each record in the form [word] [number], or none on a line of its own when the file holds no records.

Ask the user for a word to find in the file data.txt, which holds one word,number record per line. Look at every record and display [word] is [its number], or no record when none matches, then checked [how many records you looked at] on the next line.

A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line, and may be empty. Read it and display no records when it holds none, or total [every number added up], then best [the word on the record with the highest number] on the next line.

stations.name: Putting it together
stations.fact: Skipping blank lines is worth doing every time: a stray newline at the end of a file is very common.
stations.challenge: Plan the two files a sales report program would need.

rows: A file called data.txt is already there, holding one word,first,second record per line, and may be empty. Make a file called out.txt holding a line of [word] [the first number times the second] for each record, then total [all those values added up] on the last line. Close it, read it back and display the whole of it.

Ask the user for a limit. The file data.txt is already there, holding one word,number record per line: make a file called picked.txt holding a line of [word] [number] for each record whose number is above the limit. Then read picked.txt back and display [every line in it], then picked [how many] on the last line.

Each line of members.txt holds a name and an age, separated by a comma. Write a program that prints the name of every member aged 16 or over.
